Total funding is $503.6 million against $509.7 million of expenditure, but the defining fact is that $218.8 million of that leaves the building: the PA-18 special education distribution to local districts alone is $183,872,500, up $10.3 million or 5.9%. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The FY2025-26 original budget of **Oakland Schools** — the intermediate school district, one of 56 ISDs established in Michigan in 1962, serving 28 constituent districts including Troy. Dated 04.01.2025 and filed in Troy's May 20, 2025 packet because state law requires the ISD board to submit its proposed budget to every constituent district board for review and comment no later than May 1.

The enterprise numbers
Total funding **$503.6 million**: property taxes $259.9M; other local and investment revenue $48.0M; state sources $24.7M; other financing and indirect $14.0M; estimated grant awards $157.0M.

Total expenditures **$509.7 million**: salary, wage and benefits $87.1M; purchased services, supplies, utilities and dues $25.6M; capital outlay $17.8M; **transfers to LEAs and other funds $218.8M**; grant-related $157.0M; debt payments $3.4M. Both figures are net of eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund inter-company activity.

Most of this budget is a pass-through. Transfers to local districts plus grant expenditure are $375.8M of the $509.7M total.

The money that reaches districts
- **PA-18 base distribution — $183,872,500**, up $10.3 million or 5.9%, driven by the 3.7% property tax growth. Forecast to reach $206,953,100 by 2030-31.
- **Medicaid billing — ~$15.6 million** transferred to LEAs; Oakland Schools is the biller and keeps only operating costs.
- Career-focused LEA transfers and subsidies — $6,270,300, including $1,800,000 of transportation reimbursement.
- LEA support in special education — $2,450,000 for group home, medical, incarcerated youth, startup, extraordinary contingency, assistive technology and Section 24 payments.

Property tax, the engine
Budgeted to rise 3.7%, or $9,273,900, to $259,920,000 — a conservative estimate against Oakland County Equalization's projected 4%+ growth. Taxable values reached pre-recession levels in 2022-23. The district has taken a **Headlee rollback in eight of the last nine years**. The tax base is 70% principal residence, 30% non-principal residence. By fund: General Education $15,443,100; Special Education $196,433,600; Career Focused $48,043,300 — a millage allocation of 6% / 75.5% / 18.5%. A Michigan Tax Tribunal reserve of 0.25% of tax revenue, about $649,800, is budgeted against unsettled claims.

The three major funds
**General Education (100)** — revenue $27,169,800, expenditure $26,343,000, operating surplus $826,800, ending fund balance $12,888,900. Property taxes are only 57% of its revenue. Includes a new $1,000,000 Artificial Intelligence placeholder. The five-year forecast turns negative in 2028-29 and reaches $(912,883) by 2030-31, with unassigned fund balance falling from 19.1% to 11.9%.

**Special Education (200)** — revenue $209,356,700, expenditure $209,360,600, essentially break-even at $(3,900). Property taxes are 94% of revenue. Ending fund balance $21,193,800, of which **$20,000,000 is restricted for future special education center facility renovations**. Policy holds the operating restricted balance at 5% and releases the excess: the FY2024 audit exceeded target, so a supplemental $5.6 million went out to districts in December 2024.

**Career Focused Education (600)** — revenue $55,806,600, expenditure $56,050,900, deficit $(244,300). Operates four technical campuses serving ~2,700 students across 18 state CTE program codes. Campus operations $25,087,300.

People and pensions
640.0 → 641.4 FTE, a net increase of 1.3. A 2.0% across-the-board raise plus step increases; the collective bargaining agreement expires June 30, 2027. Eight MPSERS rates apply; the most common (Basic/MIP with Premium Subsidy) falls from 31.36% to 29.91%, but the **UAAL stabilization rate rises from 10.58% to 15.02%**, so the total charged rate rises from 41.94% to 44.93%. Oakland Schools' own blended rate is 28.56%. Health care runs under the hard cap — HB 6058 raises the 2025 cap 7% — with employees contributing about 18% on average.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the complete FY2025-26 original budget of **Oakland Schools**, the intermediate school district serving Oakland County. It is not Troy School District's budget; it appears in Troy's May 20, 2025 board packet because Michigan law requires the ISD board, not later than May 1, to submit its proposed budget for the next fiscal year to the board of each constituent district for review and comment. The document is dated 04.01.2025 and runs to roughly 100 pages of enterprise summary, fund-by-fund analysis, five-year forecasts and line-item schedules.

Oakland Schools describes itself as one of 56 ISDs established in Michigan in 1962 — regional service agencies providing support services to constituent district personnel that are best delivered regionally by cost, size and quality advantage — and as an autonomous, tax-supported public school district governed by Michigan General School Law. It serves 28 districts. Its stated objectives are increasing student achievement, serving the diverse needs of schools, and decreasing costs and increasing efficiencies.

**The enterprise picture.** Total proposed funding for FY2025-26 is $503.6 million: property taxes $259.9 million; other local revenue and investment revenue $48.0 million; state source revenue $24.7 million; other financing sources and indirect revenue $14.0 million; and estimated grant award funding $157.0 million. Total proposed expenditures are $509.7 million: salary, wage and benefits $87.1 million; purchased services, supplies, utilities and dues/fees $25.6 million; capital outlay $17.8 million; transfers to LEAs and other funds $218.8 million; grant-related expenditures $157.0 million; and payment on existing debt $3.4 million. Both sides are presented net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund amounts.

The structural fact worth holding onto is that this is largely a pass-through organization. Transfers to LEAs and other funds ($218.8M) plus grant-related expenditure ($157.0M) come to $375.8 million of the $509.7 million total. Oakland Schools' own salaries and operations are $87.1 million plus $25.6 million.

**Property tax revenue** drives the General Education, Special Education and Career Focused Education Funds. It is budgeted to increase 3.7%, or $9,273,900, to $259,920,000 — deliberately conservative against Oakland County Equalization projections of just over 4.0% growth, held until actual taxable values are available. Taxable values had been increasing incrementally for twelve years and finally reached pre-recession levels in 2022-23. Tax abatements leveled off after peaking in fiscal 2012 and 2013, but tax tribunal challenges increased in 2023-24, and the district monitors open cases with Oakland County Equalization and holds reserves against anticipated losses. The Michigan Tax Tribunal reserve for FY2025-26 is budgeted at 0.25% of tax revenues, approximately $649,800; unfavorable judgments return funds to the taxpayer with no recoupment from the State. The tax base is 70% principal residence and 30% non-principal residence classification property, and **the district experienced a Headlee rollback in eight of the last nine years**. By fund the property tax revenue is General Education $15,443,100 (up $551,000), Special Education $196,433,600 (up $7,008,700) and Career Focused Education $48,043,300 (up $1,714,200) — each exactly 3.70%. The stated millage allocation across the three funds is 6% / 75.5% / 18.5%.

Investment revenue is budgeted down about 15% across all funds to a total of $7,535,100, after improving significantly in 2023-24; the reduction is attributed to economic uncertainty. Other local revenue is essentially flat at $40,505,200, down 0.6%. State source revenue falls 9.8% to $24,658,900, with Section 81 ISD Operations up 2.0% but Sections 147a(3), 147a(4) and 147c(2) removed as one-time 2024-25 funding and Section 147g MPSERS 3% Healthcare Reimbursement budgeted at zero pending appropriation. Grant award funding falls 10.6% to $156,990,000 on funding uncertainties and expected carryover.

**PA-18 special education funding** is the largest single line in the document. Oakland Schools receives property tax revenue for special education and distributes it to local districts. With 3.7% tax growth projected, the base distribution to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $10.3 million, or 5.9%, to **$183,872,500**. Additional distributions may be made based on 2024-25 final audited results. The mechanism is set by fund balance policy: the Special Education Fund targets a 5% restricted balance and releases the excess to LEAs after the audit. The FY2024 audited balance exceeded that target, so a supplemental PA-18 distribution of $5.6 million was distributed in December 2024, out of a $9.8 million supplemental budget carried in FY2024-25 and not repeated in FY2025-26. The five-year forecast projects the base distribution at $188,623,200 in 2026-27, $192,979,500 in 2027-28, $197,470,200 in 2028-29, $202,113,600 in 2029-30 and $206,953,100 in 2030-31.

**Medicaid.** The Medicaid Billing Services program provides billing services to all school districts and is expected to generate approximately **$15.6 million of revenue for LEAs** in FY2025-26. The Medicaid Fund 273 shows revenue of $16,328,500 — Medicaid Service Fees $13,303,400, Caring 4 Students service fees $859,600, federal Medicaid Outreach Fees $1,412,800, cost recovery fees $288,000, interest $394,600, and MPSERS state revenue $70,100 — against expenditures of the same $16,328,500, of which transfers to LEAs are $15.6 million and the balance is $353,600 of salaries, $257,900 of benefits and about $22,700 of facility operations. By design the fund carries no committed fund balance: all Medicaid revenue less operating cost is distributed to participating districts.

**Financial subsidies for cooperative services** are reported under Board Policy 3230 and total $1,364,800: Xello career cruising software $360,000; CDX Automotive software $31,400; Nepris industry connections platform $250,000; Lightcast Alumni Pathways $45,000; Illuminate DnA student assessment $354,700; Discovery Education Streaming $77,600; Atlas Rubicon curriculum management $199,500; and STAMP proficiency assessments $46,600. These exclude the cost of staff FTE providing direct district support.

**Staffing and personnel costs.** Total FTE moves from 640.0 to 641.4, a net increase of 1.3: adding 1.0 FTE Senior HR Generalist overlapping the HR Manager position for one year until it is eliminated at the end of 2025-26; adding 1.0 FTE split between District & School Services and Special Populations for a Universal Design for Learning Consultant; and reducing 0.7 FTE of part-time staff in Student Services and Special Populations. An across-the-board pay increase of 2.0% is budgeted for all staff, consistent with the collective bargaining agreement expiring June 30, 2027, plus step increases — a 1.2% growth rate on the non-union wage base and about 0.9% on the union base. Total salary and wages with FICA rise 4.6% to $55,710,900.

**MPSERS.** Eight retirement rates are in effect depending on hire date and benefit election. For October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025 the most common plan — Basic/MIP with Premium Subsidy — is charged 31.36% on reported payroll plus a 10.58% UAAL stabilization rate, totalling 41.94%. For October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026, per the Governor's proposed budget, the payroll rate falls to 29.91% but **the UAAL stabilization rate rises to 15.02%**, so the total charged rate rises to 44.93%. Oakland Schools analyzed its own employees' elections and projects a blended rate exclusive of UAAL of 28.56% for 2025-26 — the district pays an additional $28.56 in retirement cost for every $100 of wages — forecast to rise 1.0% annually. Total MPSERS retirement costs are $21,886,800.

**Health care** runs under the hard cap, adjusted annually on January 1 by the medical consumer price index. In 2024-25 the Michigan Legislature passed House Bill 6058 increasing the 2025 hard cap by 7%; the bill had not been presented to the Governor at printing but the increase is included. Medical CPI growth of 4.5% is budgeted for 2025-26. The resulting limits for plan years beginning after 1/1/25 and 1/1/26 are: Family $22,523.34 then $23,536.89; Individual plus one $17,271.14 then $18,048.34; Single $8,258.54 then $8,630.17. Employees pay all costs of their plan choice exceeding these limits and are expected to contribute about 18% on average. Total healthcare insurance cost is $7,417,900.

**What's new in this budget.** A new Artificial Intelligence unit within Technology Services (location 031) carries a $1,000,000 placeholder budget in the General Education Fund pending determination of staffing, professional services and technology needs — the primary driver of that fund's purchased services rising about 22%. The OSTC technical campus renovations continue: Phase I upgraded secured entrances with Welcome Centers at all four campuses; Phase II covers corridor refresh and parking lot replacement with security gates, completing Summer 2025. Oakland Schools is providing up to $5 million for Literacy Essentials Oakland, and has launched a Numeracy Initiative (EPIC) in response to declining 3rd-to-6th grade Mathematics M-STEP performance, running PDSA cycles in 13 classrooms across 12 schools and 10 districts. A Business Office Residency Program begun June 2024 trains a cohort of four toward Michigan School Business Officials certification; an HR Leadership Academy launched 2024-25 runs a parallel two-year model. Both are fully funded by the General Education Fund. Mental health work continues across Tier 1 supports, PREPaRE training (499 educators in workshop 1 across 23 of 28 districts; 368 in workshop 2 across all 28), Behavioral Threat Assessment and Management (557 educators from 22 districts and 26 resource officers), and comprehensive suicide prevention (252 educators), with continuing consultation to Oxford Community Schools.

**Budget policy and control.** Policies 3050, 3100, 3150 and 3170 govern. The Superintendent plans and executes the budget; changes must come through the amendment process at least three times each fiscal year for Board review. Fund balance targets are: General Education Fund unassigned 7.5% to 12.5% of operating expenditures; Career Focused Education Fund restricted 7.5% to 12.5%; Special Education Fund restricted 5% to 10% of expected operating expenditures less transfers to local districts; all others at the Superintendent's determination. The Superintendent may transfer between line items within a fund but inter-fund transfers require prior Board approval. Legal requirements cited are the General Property Tax Act (PA 206 of 1893, MCL 211.24e), the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act (PA 2 of 1968), and the Revised School Code (PA 451 of 1976, MCL 380.624 and 380.684). Budgets must be adopted no later than June 30 following a public hearing, via a general appropriations resolution; once approved, expenditures cannot exceed budget by function without Board amendment. The financial system will not allow funds to be encumbered or paid beyond the budgetary control account, and a quarterly financial reporting package goes to the Board including budget-to-actual reports, cash and investment position, check register by fund, procurement card activity and biweekly expense reimbursements.

**Cost allocation.** Costs are allocated across the three major funds under MDE's rules for ISD use of special education funds, with a 25% maximum allocation cap on each eligible function-based cost pool for the Special Education Fund; the Career Focused Education Fund has no such rule but is treated the same way. The general allocation is 50% GEF / 25% SEF / 25% CFEF. Where a department generates revenue — predominantly Technology Services — the gross pool is reduced by that revenue first, and Technology Licensing is allocated 70/15/15. Activity-based methods apply elsewhere: FTE-based 24/24/52 for Financial Services, Human Resources, Procurement and Enterprise Technical Services; space utilization 50/24/26 for facilities; transportation miles 73/25/2 for Pupil Transportation; and property tax millage 6/75.5/18.5 for the property tax function. Allocated departments total $28,663,400 — $12,665,100 GEF, $6,910,400 SEF, $9,087,900 CFEF — or 11.15% of the three funds combined.

**General Education Fund (100).** Revenue of $27,169,800, down 2.34%, comprising local sources $19,485,000 (property taxes $15,443,100 or 57% of total revenue, investment income $1,061,100, and fee-based items including CTN $600,000, Illuminate $513,700, workshop fees $350,000 and technology application fees), state sources $6,958,800 down 9.43%, and other financing sources $726,000. Expenditures of $26,343,000, down 6.50%: General Administration $3,019,400; Finance and Operations $10,615,400; Instructional Programs and Services $10,569,000; and Plant and Fixed Charges $2,139,200, the last down 61.76% because 2024-25 carried an additional $3.0 million transfer to capital projects for roofing and boiler work. The operating surplus is $826,800, and ending fund balance $12,888,900 — assigned $8,882,100, unassigned $3,951,500, non-spendable $55,300 — with unassigned at 15% of budgeted expenditures. The five-year forecast shows surpluses of $886,000 in 2026-27 and $402,900 in 2027-28, then deficits of $(180,800), $(585,573) and $(912,883), with end-of-year unassigned fund balance as a percentage of expenditure running 18.3%, 19.1%, 17.8%, 15.3% and 11.9% — falling below the 12.5% policy top of range only at the end. The separate General Education funded projects and grants fund (105) budgets $94,840,000 of revenue and expenditure, down 15.70%, of which payments to other public schools are $56,767,800 and payments to not-for-profit entities $21,703,400.

**Special Education Fund (200).** Revenue of $209,356,700, up 2.90%: local sources $199,640,300 (property taxes $196,433,600 or 94% of total revenue, investment income $3,136,700), state sources $9,466,400 including Section 51a $4,622,600 and State Payment in Lieu of Taxes $2,077,400, and other financing sources $250,000. Expenditures of $209,360,600: Oakland Schools program supervision and direction $2,724,700; program operations $12,053,400; plant and fixed charges $8,260,000; **PA-18 distribution $183,872,500**; and LEA transfers and program subsidies $2,450,000. The operating result is a deficit of $(3,900) — by construction, since the PA-18 distribution is the balancing item. Ending fund balance is $21,193,800: $20,000,000 restricted for future special education center facility renovations and available for center program operators to request, $1,152,000 restricted for special education operations, and $41,800 non-spendable. The restricted operating balance sits at 5% of expenditures net of LEA transfers, against a 2023-24 actual of 32.6% before the supplemental distributions drew it down. The separate special education grants fund (205) budgets $60,155,000, of which federal sources are $57,455,000 and payments to other public schools $50,756,000, plus $2,842,000 for non-public school pupils. Special Populations serves approximately 25,100 students with an IEP through four service delivery areas — capacity building, student services for low incidence, compliance support, and the Materials Center with its Braille and large print library.

**Career Focused Education Fund (600).** Revenue of $55,806,600, up 0.97%: local sources $49,493,800 (property taxes $48,043,300 or 86% of revenue, investment income $1,007,200, early college tuition $348,000), state sources $6,269,800 down 13.50% including Section 61a.1 $1,727,500 and MPSERS categoricals, and other financing sources $43,000 including $25,000 from Wayne RESA for Section 107 adult education compliance. Expenditures of $56,050,900, down 4.29%: campus operations $25,087,300; district and campus support operations $4,539,000; LEA transfers and program subsidies $6,270,300; and plant and fixed charges $20,154,300. The deficit is $(244,300) and ending fund balance $4,647,100, with the restricted component at $4,618,000, about 8% of expenditures.

The fund operates four Oakland Schools Technical Campuses serving approximately 2,700 students from all 28 districts, running 18 state CTE program codes: agriculture (501), marketing sales and service (510), culinary arts (523), education general (524), cosmetology (531), public safety (538), construction trades (540), line worker (541), cyber security (548), collision repair (549), automobile technician (550), medium and heavy truck technician (551), graphics and printing (562), machine tool technology (564), welding (566), mechatronics (575), therapeutic services (580) and computer programming (595) — the collision, automobile and truck programs NATEF certified. Campus totals are Northwest $5,810,300, Southeast $6,139,900, Northeast $6,893,600 and Southwest $6,243,500. LEA transfers include a Career Readiness allocation of $3,650,100, transportation support of $1,800,000, NAIS lab support of $476,300, camps $100,000 and STEM $131,300; the STEMi mobile classroom carries $504,400 of operating cost and is fully booked at all 28 districts and academies. Regional programs total $4.4 million annually through the forecast. One School Resource Officer per campus is provided under an arrangement with the Oakland County Sheriff's Department; a Michigan State Police grant partially reimbursed the cost, but from 2026-27 all SROs are 100% locally funded. Campus renovation debt service runs about $2.5 million annually through 2036, with forecast transfers out to debt service of $2.6 to $3.3 million annually from 2026-27 through 2030-31. The five-year restricted fund balance forecast runs 7.0%, 7.7%, 7.6%, 11.3% and 13.5%.

**Special revenue funds.** The Shared Services and Tuition Programs Fund 270 is a cost-recovery fund covering VLAC K-8 and 9-12, the Accelerated College Experience, Graduation Alliance, shared services and the foreign exchange program, with revenue of $20,541,600 against expenditure of $20,562,300 and a committed ending balance of $5,146,700; shared services alone is $11,424,900 of revenue against $14,093,600 of expenditure. Tuition rates are unchanged from 2024-25: VLAC K-8 at $6,450 resident and $6,650 non-resident on a projected 240 FTE; VLAC 9-12 at $6,700 and $6,900 on 250 FTE; and ACE at $4,900 on an estimated 290 students, where students attend both their district high school and Oakland Community College and can earn up to 60 transferable credits, an associate degree or a certificate through a thirteenth year. The Oakland Network for Education Fund 271 operates a fiber-based data network connecting 29 consortium members, with revenue of $1,589,300 against expenditure of $1,238,900 and a committed balance of $14,377,000; a $1.9 million infrastructure update spanning 2023-24 and 2024-25 completes by June 30, 2025, and the fund also carries Literacy Essentials Oakland and EPIC Math at $300,000 each. The HR/Finance Consortium Fund 277 supports the MiPEER ERP consortium of 20 districts running BusinessPlus with an 18-member support team, with revenue of $1,374,900 against expenditure of $1,305,400 and a committed balance of $840,000; Oakland Schools transferred a net $4,875,000 from the CPDI Fund between FY2012-13 and FY2015-16 to subsidize per-student cost, and a $0.7 million ONE Fund startup grant was repaid in installments through 2023-24. The School Activities Fund 290, created in 2019-20 under GASB 84, budgets $180,000 on both sides with a $257,400 ending balance.

**Debt service.** Three funds. Fund 311, 2016 Refunding Bonds, accounts for the partial refunding of the 2007 CFE Campus Renovation Bonds — the unrefunded remainder was paid off in May 2017 — with a payment schedule through 2036 at approximately $3.3 million annually and a restricted balance of $9,898,900. Fund 313 accounts for the 2010 Qualified School Construction Bond that funded Administration Building and CFE campus renovations, running through 2027, with a restricted balance of $477,400; in 2024-25 the five funds that benefited from the original issuance provided additional resources to strengthen its position. Fund 314 is the QSCB Construction Reserve holding required annual set-aside payments, with a restricted balance of $12,888,800, which on maturity in 2027 will pay the bond principal. Combined debt service expenditure is $3,387,200 — principal $1,610,000 and interest $1,777,200.

**Capital projects.** Fund 404, CFE Technical Campus Renovations Phase II, budgets $7.3 million of revenue including a $6.7 million transfer from the Career Focused Education Fund against $12.7 million of expenditure, drawing the committed balance from $18,608,400 to $7,941,500; significant 2025-26 projects are the campus corridor refresh and parking lot replacements. Fund 406, Administration Building Renovation and Maintenance, budgets $0.8 million of revenue against $3.4 million of expenditure including roof and boiler replacement, with the balance falling to $10,560,700. Total capital outlay across all funds is $17,748,000, down 16.1%, agreeing to the Board-approved five-year capital outlay plan presented for first reading April 1, 2025.

**Enterprise and internal service.** The Production Print Enterprise Fund 710 budgets about $1.1 million on both sides and carries a negative total net position of $(893,800), a consequence of retroactively applying GASB 68 and GASB 75 in FY2020-21 and recording the fund's share of statewide pension and OPEB liabilities; in 2024-25 administration scaled the print shop down, discontinuing business with county, city and township governments to focus on constituent districts while raising prices incrementally toward self-sustainability. The Risk Related Activity Fund 810, the internal service fund holding all district insurances, projects a net position of $3,100,500 — professional liability claim fluctuation reserve $1,240,000, cyber liability $1,278,400, property/casualty settlement contingency $50,000 and retained earnings $532,100. Compensated absence liabilities are 100% funded through June 30, 2024, with balance sheet accruals of $3.5 million, and the district is implementing GASB 101 for the year ending June 30, 2025.

**Economic context.** The document describes Oakland County as one of the most prosperous counties in the country, with knowledge-based economic activity among the most concentrated nationally and an above-average share of residents holding an associate degree or better. Unemployment was 3.8% at December 31, 2024 against a 4.1% national average. 94% of county jobs are private sector. Job recovery by the end of 2026 is expected to exceed pre-pandemic levels by 7.7% in blue-collar and 2.0% in higher-education service jobs, while lower-education service industries remain below pre-pandemic levels. The county's Oakland80 initiative targets 80% of adults holding a post-secondary degree or credential by 2030.
